1:
How far this prophecy reaches is the opening question, and the answers are far apart. Adam Clarke holds the images too bold to be confined to history: it is impossible, without great violence to symbolical language, to restrain them to the calamities that fell on the Edomites under Nebuchadnezzar or to anything the enemies of the Church have suffered since; Edom must therefore be a type of the last great adversary, and the prophecy, in its ultimate meaning, remains to be accomplished. He allows the devastation by Nebuchadnezzar may be primarily in view, but says that event, so far as we have any account of it, by no means comes up to the terms of the prophecy, and that it is hard to see how the next chapter’s flourishing state could follow from it. Charles Ellicott reads the two chapters as a closing epilogue to the first great collection, written in a transition period with the Assyrian attack now in the background: in the destruction of that army the prophet sees a pledge of the fate of all who fight God, and fixes on Edom as the representative instance, the inscriptions showing they submitted to the invader and probably had a part in the attack on Jerusalem. He treats the picture of carcasses covering the earth as hyperbole. Keil and Delitzsch stand nearer Clarke: these chapters are an apocalyptic finale carrying us away from the stage of history, the shapes of the present spiritualised into something ideal, so that we are set down in the midst of the last things. They add that this very difference of impression has raised doubts about the authenticity of the closing prophecy, and answer that the relation later prophets stand in to it drives those doubts away.

John Gill clears away two readings of the summons. It is not addressed to the Jews, as some suppose who find here their destruction after rejecting the Messiah; still less is it a call to hear the Gospel, as one interpreter thinks, since it is not good news but bad that the hearers are summoned to. John Calvin makes a different point about the audience. The address is to the Gentiles, but the prophet has his eye principally on the Church, since otherwise he would have spoken to the deaf; these things were said not for the Edomites, who would pay no regard, but for the comfort of the godly who were being harassed. Calvin adds that heaven and earth are called as witnesses because the judgment will be so visible that even the dumb creatures shall behold it, and that the prophets regularly address them when men, though endued with reason, are stupid. Matthew Henry says it more sharply: the inanimate products of the earth are called to as more likely to hearken than sinners, whose hearts are hardened.

On the slaughter the notes are practical. Calvin observes that when a few are slain they are committed to the earth, but when so great a multitude falls at once there are not enough left to bury them, adding shame to the slaughter; and takes the blood running from the mountains as a figure of escape cut off everywhere, the sword raging as cruelly on the heights as on the field. He also notices the tense: the prophet speaks of things future in the past, to set the event immediately before people lying low under adversity. Henry reads the whole as a proclamation of war, the armies of the nations before God’s fury being as dry stubble before a consuming fire however numerous, and draws the counsel that a time is prefixed for the deliverance of the Church, so that we must wait till then and judge nothing before the time. John Wesley widens the reference in a line: the indignation falls not only on the Assyrians but on all the enemies of God’s people.
4:
The dissolving of the host of heaven is taken by none as astronomy. John Calvin states the rule: these things relate to men’s apprehension, for heaven is not moved out of its place, and when God manifests his anger we are terrified as though he folded up the heavens, though nothing of the kind happens there. He puts it in the second person—you will be seized with such terror that you will think the sky is falling on your heads—and adds that it is the just punishment of indifference that men who fear no God tremble at the rustling of a falling leaf. John Wesley generalises this into a rule: prophetic writers in either Testament describe great calamities in words belonging to the day of judgment, and the deliverances of God’s people in expressions belonging to the resurrection. Charles Ellicott notes that no picture of a day of the Lord was complete without this symbolism, and finds its point in the contrast between the transitory sun, moon and stars and the eternity of God—where the Greek poets said the generations of men are as leaves, this prophet sees even the host of heaven falling like a leaf.

Why the sword should be bathed in heaven troubles two of them. Adam Clarke calls the received reading improper, since the sword was to be glutted not in the heavens but in Edom, and in heaven was only prepared; he reports an emendation and rejects it as premature, then notes that one old version has instead that the sword shall be revealed, and says frankly that whatever its translator read, he will follow the sense given. John Gill reads the heaven here as the jurisdiction whose chief men the vengeance strikes first. Ellicott renders the verb literally as having drunk to the full, observes that where the sword is elsewhere soaked with blood this one is bathed in heaven, and suggests the difference may be the dipping by which steel was tempered; he also prefers for Edom to upon Idumea, no reason being assignable for the Greek form. Calvin meets the difficulty by looking at the decree rather than the act: the prophet has in view the secret purpose of God, which appoints everything before it is executed, so that the sword by which the wicked will be slain is already bloody in his sight while they are untouched—as Sodom was already burning in his sight while it indulged in wine and feasting. Edom is singled out, he adds, because they were enemies though related by blood and marked with the same religion, and he applies it to his own century, where the deadliest enemies share the same baptism and profess the same Christ.

The sacrifice is where Calvin is candid. The slaughter is called a sacrifice because sacrifices are offered for God’s honour, and the destruction of the wicked tends the same way; but he does not pretend the figure comfortable. Sacrifices, he says, were not pleasant to behold, since the taking of life, the reeking blood and the stench of the smoke might repel a spectator, and yet in these the honour of God shone brightly—and just so this slaughter was hideous and little fitted to obtain regard, so believers must lift their eyes to heaven. Clarke traces a line of dependence: a later prophet manifestly imitated this passage, setting out the adverse leaders under the same emblems and adding boldness by having God summon every bird and beast to the feast; and the author of a still later vision took the image from that prophet rather than this one. Keil and Delitzsch single out one phrase, that to contend for Zion is a flash of lightning throwing light on the obscurity of the prophecy backwards and forwards. Wesley reads the sword’s filling as a metaphor from a glutton, and takes the lambs, goats and rams for people of every rank.
7:
The animal named in the seventh verse is identified four ways. John Gill says it is either the rhinoceros, as some hold, there being no such creature as the unicorn, or else the buffalo. Adam Clarke reports that one bishop translated it wild goats and a scholar took it for a wild goat of the deserts of Arabia, but thinks it generally means the rhinoceros. Charles Ellicott prefers the aurochs or wild bull, and lists the identifications made—the buffalo, an antelope, and, on the strength of Assyrian inscriptions and bas-reliefs, a particular species of wild ox proposed by a naturalist who was also a scholar. He adds that the verb translated shall come down implies going down to the shambles. John Wesley is content that it was a beast of great strength and fierceness, standing here for princes and potentates. John Calvin guards the other end of the list: it should not seem strange that lambs are mingled with savage beasts, since the word commends no mildness but is used comparatively, of the feeble sort; and his annotator adds the grim note that such men will be sacrificed by hands as wicked as their own.

On the year of recompences Adam Clarke changes the sense of the phrase. Deriving one noun as another is derived, he renders it the year of recompense to the defender of the cause of Zion, and reports an old version that has simply the Judge of Zion. Calvin thinks the verse indispensable rather than incidental: it states the object God has in view, without which the preceding threats might have seemed obscure, since it would be uncertain knowledge if we did not see that in punishing the wicked God testifies his care to preserve his own people. He insists the Edomites stand for a class, so that what is said of them extends to all the Church’s enemies, and finds in the words day and year a reminder that God does not sleep but delays vengeance to a fit season, that believers may possess their souls in patience meanwhile.

Matthew Henry takes the burning country three ways at once, and marks his own uncertainty about the third. It describes, first, the melancholy changes providence often makes in countries and cities, so that we cannot now find where many great towns celebrated in history once stood; second, the judgments falling on enemies who aim to ruin the Church and infallibly ruin themselves; and third, the final desolation of this world, reserved unto fire—the earth itself, he says, when it and all its works are burnt up, will, for aught he knows, be turned into a hell to those who set their affections on earthly things. He finds the cause in the guilt: so combustible has sin made their land that it takes fire at the first spark of wrath struck upon it. Calvin reads the same verses as plainly hyperbolical and defends the manner: the Lord is compelled to speak so, since plain words would make no impression, and the prophets treated of things dark and secret, generally thought incredible, so that many supposed they spoke at random and much confirmation was needed. He also notices what the passage does not say. The unquenched fire cuts off all hope of pardon from these enemies, and the contrast must be supplied by the reader, since some mitigation is always held out to the people of God for their comfort. Keil and Delitzsch read the land in a geographical and at once an emblematical sense, and describe the desolation by the measure and level of the primeval chaos, the monarchy gone and no nobles left to elect one. Gill applies the long burning to the fall of a later city, and Wesley says only that the country will be dealt with as the cities of the plain were, and left a spectacle of vengeance to all succeeding ages.
11:
The creatures that take over the ruin divide those who work at the zoology from one who refuses to. John Calvin says twice that opinions vary and Hebrew commentators are not agreed, and that it would serve no purpose to be uneasy about exact meanings, since it is enough to understand the prophet’s design, to describe a desert haunted by hideous creatures that do not dwell with men. Adam Clarke takes the opposite course and names them all. The first is the pelican, named from a verb meaning to vomit, on the story that she swallows shellfish, kills them with the heat of her stomach, throws up the shells and eats the fish; the second the hedgehog; the third a bird named from a root meaning to blow, from its noise like the lowing of an ox. Later he supplies mountain cats and jackals, and takes the creature of the fifteenth verse for a serpent named from its leap on its prey. On the ostrich he quotes a traveller who says they roar sometimes like a lion, sometimes like a bull, and that he had often heard them groan as if in distress. Charles Ellicott reports that naturalists agree on pelicans and hedgehogs, the owl and raven, but takes the later names into another region: they belong, apparently, to mythical zoology, the satyr conveying a demon-brute of the waste places, and the screech owl being the night-demon of the legends, the first man’s first wife, turned into a demon when she left him and among later Jews the bugbear of the nursery; night-vampire, he suggests, would be the best rendering. John Gill keeps the doubt, reporting that authorities disagree whether two of the names mean the same bird and that it is hard to say what is designed.

The measuring line raises another question, and Clarke finds the text broken. One word attached to the twelfth verse, he says, embarrasses it and makes it inexplicable—he knows of no tolerable explanation yet given, nor of anyone who has made out the construction—so he joins it to the previous verse and supplies a letter or two that seem lost. Ellicott explains the instrument rather than the text: the line and stones are the builder’s plumb-line, used not for building up but for destroying with a kind of scientific completeness, the two words for confusion and emptiness being those of the primeval chaos. John Wesley puts it in a workman’s terms, that the line marks out what is to be pulled down. Calvin reports that some give the phrase an opposite sense and apply it to the Jews, prefers the simpler view that it belongs with the rest to the Edomites, and cites a later prophet who uses the same word, whose passage he calls an approbation of this prophecy.

The failure of the monarchy is read historically by one, rhetorically by another. Ellicott observes that the kingship of Edom seems to have been elective, its rulers known by another title, and that no chief in the recorded list is the son of his predecessor—so the prophet foretells neither electors nor anyone to elect. Keil and Delitzsch say the same in a phrase, that there is no longer a monarchy for the nobles to elect. Calvin declines to canvass the readings—the passage has had various interpretations, he says, which he does not quote because refuting them would be tedious—and takes the line as raillery against a nation’s pride cherished by long peace. On the thorns in the palaces he is sharpest: God punishes the insolence of men who built lofty houses so that their memory might be handed down, by banishing the builders and turning the dwellings into nests of birds and dens of beasts, so that instead of trophies of their name they stand as monuments of foolish ambition, animals supplying the place of men and representing their dispositions.
16:
What the book of the Lord is nobody agrees, and John Gill lays out four answers. One Jewish interpreter takes it for the book of the law, where the punishment of God’s enemies is threatened; a second for Genesis, where every creature with its mate came to Noah in the ark; a third for the book of God’s decrees, in which, could it be seen, all the particulars of this prophecy might be read. Gill prefers the prophecy of Isaiah itself, which, read when these things come to pass, will let anyone see by comparing events with predictions how exactly everything is accomplished—and he draws a corollary, that the book being called the book of the Lord shows it was written by divine inspiration. Keil and Delitzsch agree, saying the prophet applied the title to his own collection of prophecies, so that whoever lived to see the judgment fall would need only look into that writing; and they explain the two prepositions, one for entering a thing in a book, what is written being placed on the page, and one for searching in a book, since a man leans over it. Charles Ellicott calls the phrase exceptional and leaves the choice open between this section and the whole collection.

John Calvin takes the option the others pass over. He reports the reading that makes it this prophecy, and another that makes it the eternal decree, which he calls ingenious but not sufficiently natural, and settles on the Law, called the book of the Lord by way of eminence, since from it as from their source the prophets drew their doctrine. That reading gives him his point: lest the strangeness of the event keep men from believing it, the prophet reminds them they had been warned long before, and so censures those who stared at the announcement as something uncommon, since he brings nothing new but confirms what was declared long since. Adam Clarke spends his note on manuscript variants—five copies reading the divine name where the text has a pronoun, several editions a different verb form, fourteen a masculine pronoun for a feminine—and admits that to see their importance the Hebrew must be consulted. John Wesley notices the abrupt change of person, frequent here, and reads the gathering of the creatures as done by an instinct put into them, as when they were brought of old to the first man and to Noah.

Ellicott adds a caution about the fulfilment the others do not. Travellers have supplied illustrations of the country, which swarms with snakes while the desolate heights are inherited by wild crows and eagles; but it has to be remembered, he says, that the decay was very gradual, since the ruins of the chief cities are of Roman origin and indicate a period of culture and prosperity reaching far into the history of the Empire. On the casting of the lot Calvin turns the verse on the reader. If the beasts hold their possession by allotment, the whole country is at God’s disposal, to drive out inhabitants and grant it to whom he pleases; from which it follows that no one may promise himself a permanent abode except so far as he has his place by lot, and on the express condition of leaving it the moment God calls. We lead a dependent life wherever he supports us, and on our native soil or far from it we are strangers alike. Then he turns it to comfort: if God keeps wild beasts in the possession he allotted them, how much more will he preserve men, for whose sake he made heaven, earth and the seas? Ellicott makes the point historically, that God is here the supreme ruler assigning every nation its place and its seasons of prosperity and judgment, and Wesley compares the division to a land once divided among a people by lot and line.
